prompt.context: Two large branded pharmaceutical companies are merging. The head of development (pre-clinical and clinical) has a declining budget and wants to re-think his portfolio. He currently uses a spreadsheet to evaluate his portfolio which contains columns for the chemical name, estimated launch date, and lead indication.
prompt.question: Your client wants you to add a column for the current market value of the partially developed drug so that he can evaluate which ones to push through development. How do you do it?

clarifying_info.q: How many drugs are in the development portfolio?
clarifying_info.a: There are 60 drugs in development: 1/3 in clinical trials and 2/3 in pre-clinical development.

clarifying_info.q: What is the typical timeline to bring a drug to market?
clarifying_info.a: It takes 10 years to bring a drug from pre-clinical to launch, and there is large attrition along the way.

clarifying_info.q: Are we considering global or U.S. launch? Any bundling or combination therapies?
clarifying_info.a: Assume U.S. launch only, no bundling, and each compound represents a novel therapy.

framework: Frame the problem as an NPV calculation: determine value = PV(future cash flows) adjusted for probability of success at each development phase
Revenue side: estimate market size at time of launch, then determine the compound's market share
Cost side: identify fixed costs (facilities, R&D) and variable costs (manufacturing, sales & marketing launch costs)
Discount free cash flows back to the present at an appropriate rate
Adjust each year's cash flow for attrition / probability of success at each development phase (pre-clinical, Phase I, II, III, FDA approval)
If value gaps emerge, evaluate make-or-buy options to plug the pipeline hole

questions.prompt: Walk through how you would estimate the revenue for a given drug in the portfolio.
questions.guidance: Strong answer covers: (1) total number of patients with the target disease (use sources like American Cancer Society, analyst reports); (2) project patient population forward to launch date using historical growth rates; (3) number actually treated for the disease; (4) subset using drugs vs. other procedures (surgery, etc.); (5) competitive environment — current marketed drugs, their lifecycle position at launch, pipeline competitors; (6) pricing drivers: efficacy vs. standard of care, first-in-class status, convenience/dosing, other therapies for the same indication.

questions.prompt: What costs would you include, and how would you arrive at a single NPV figure?
questions.guidance: Fixed costs: new manufacturing facilities, R&D spend remaining before launch, one-time sales and marketing launch investment. Variable costs: cost of goods manufactured. Sum revenues and costs to get annual free cash flow; discount each year's FCF back to today; separately multiply by probability of success at each phase to account for attrition. The result is the risk-adjusted NPV (rNPV) — the market value column the client wants.

math.setup: rNPV = sum over years t of [FCF_t * P(success through phase at year t)] / (1+r)^t
steps: Estimate annual revenue = (patients treated with drug) x (price per patient per year)
Subtract annual costs to get FCF per year
Multiply each year's FCF by cumulative probability of reaching that stage (e.g., pre-clinical x Phase I x Phase II x Phase III x approval)
Discount each probability-adjusted FCF at WACC
Sum all discounted probability-adjusted FCFs to get rNPV
math.answer: rNPV per compound — insert into the spreadsheet column

questions.prompt: Suppose that after completing the valuation, half the compounds in pre-clinical development turn out to have no value. How do you plug the resulting revenue gap?
questions.guidance: Frame as make-or-buy. Make options: (1) expedite development of existing higher-value pipeline drugs — acknowledge this is hard given the complex development process; (2) maximize existing marketed products — OTC switch, new indications, line extensions — note this may already be underway and unlikely to close the full gap. Buy options: (3) acquire compounds or a company to fill the hole — perform the same compound valuation on acquisition targets; also factor in synergies with the combined organization and the target company's track record in launching similar products.

brainstorming.prompt: What levers can a pharmaceutical company pull when it discovers a significant portion of its pipeline has no value?

categories.name: Make — internal development
ideas: Accelerate development of high-value existing pipeline compounds
Pursue additional indications for pipeline drugs
Invest in platform technologies to generate new candidates faster

categories.name: Make — maximize marketed products
ideas: Switch branded Rx products to OTC to expand addressable market
Seek new indications or label expansions for already-approved drugs
Reformulate for improved dosing convenience to extend product lifecycle

categories.name: Buy — external acquisition
ideas: Acquire individual compounds from smaller biotechs at various development stages
In-license late-stage assets to fill near-term gap
Acquire a company with a complementary pipeline
Form co-development partnerships to share risk and cost

recommendation: Implement a risk-adjusted NPV (rNPV) model for all 60 compounds, using disease epidemiology data, competitive intelligence, and phase-specific attrition rates to populate the new spreadsheet column

For the ~20 pre-clinical compounds with zero or negative rNPV, deprioritize them to free up budget for the higher-value compounds and pursue targeted in-licensing or bolt-on acquisitions to replenish the pipeline
risks: rNPV estimates are highly sensitive to assumed success probabilities and market-size projections — small changes can flip a compound's rank
Acquisitions made under time pressure to fill a pipeline gap risk overpaying or buying programs with hidden technical risk
Expediting development to plug the gap is generally not feasible and may increase attrition
next_steps: Build the rNPV model and rank all 60 compounds
Identify the top-priority candidates for continued investment vs. discontinuation
Scan the external market (biotech, academic spin-outs) for acquisition or in-licensing targets that complement the surviving pipeline
Align sales and marketing on revised launch timelines
